profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a startup building a bug-intelligence pipeline for open-source quantum software repositories. Overnight, their prototype flakiness detector suddenly flagged a large batch of quantum bug reports as 'likely flaky,' including reports from Qiskit Aer, Cirq, and PennyLane that the team did not expect. The meeting is between the engineer responsible for the detector service and the engineer responsible for the bug-report ingestion and normalization pipeline. Their agenda is to diagnose why the spike happened, decide whether the issue is a model problem, a data-pipeline problem, or an environment-replay problem, and choose a short-term fix before the weekly demo. The expected outcome is agreement on the most plausible root cause, what immediate mitigation to deploy, and what evidence each person will gather afterward.

members.name: Lena Park
members.expertise: NLP pipelines, weak supervision, experiment reproducibility, classifier serving
members.background: Lena joined from a tooling team that built issue-triage classifiers for classical CI failures; she now owns the service that labels bug reports as deterministic, flaky, or unclear based on report text, linked CI logs, and rerun metadata.
members.private_state: She wants to avoid reverting the new detector calibration before the demo because she has already told leadership the model upgrade reduced false negatives; she is worried the spike is being caused by upstream input drift rather than the detector itself.
hidden_assumptions: When people say a report was 'rerun,' that refers to repeated executions of the same workflow on the same commit and dependency lockfile, because that is how her detector features define rerun consistency.

The 'simulator backend' mentioned in normalized bug reports is the exact execution target named in the raw issue or CI artifact, not a family-level alias that merges Aer CPU, Aer GPU, qsim, and default.qubit.
A 'fix' for this incident means restoring the detector's previous precision profile on the benchmark slice used for the demo, even if some newly surfaced edge cases remain unresolved in ingestion.
If the pipeline says it preserved environment details, the detector still has access to the raw wording that mentions seeds, shots, and simulator flags, not just extracted fields.

members.name: Ravi Natarajan
members.expertise: CI systems, bug-report ETL, log normalization, build reproducibility
members.background: Ravi previously maintained flaky-test dashboards for a large cloud platform and now owns the pipeline that ingests GitHub issues, CI artifacts, workflow reruns, and environment metadata from quantum software projects into a normalized incident store.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the new ingestion unification rollout because it removed many repo-specific scrapers; he is concerned that the detector is overreacting to ordinary nondeterminism language in quantum projects rather than a true data defect.
hidden_assumptions: When people say a report was 'rerun,' it is enough that the test or workflow was executed again in a nearby time window, even if a dependency patch version or simulator seed changed, because his pipeline groups those as the same incident lineage.

The 'simulator backend' field is intentionally canonicalized to a framework-neutral bucket so downstream systems can compare reports across projects, and that abstraction should not affect flakiness reasoning.
A 'fix' for this incident means stopping the sudden alert spike in production triage, even if benchmark behavior changes, because operational stability is the relevant definition of fixed.
If environment details are preserved, structured metadata extracted from issue templates and CI artifacts is sufficient; keeping the original free-text section is unnecessary duplication.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the detector should compare 'reruns' to see whether the report is inconsistent.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means repeated executions of the same test/workflow on the same commit with effectively the same environment and dependency state, so inconsistency implies flakiness evidence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any subsequent execution linked to the same issue or workflow lineage within the incident window, even if the environment drifted slightly due to updated containers, dependency patch versions, or simulator seed defaults.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In CI and bug-triage work, 'rerun' is common shorthand and both participants are experienced enough to treat it as obvious; neither expects the other to include or exclude small environment changes because that boundary usually lives inside tooling, not meeting discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: Which backend the reports refer to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the spike is concentrated on the 'simulator backend.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of specific raw execution targets preserved in past training examples, such as Aer CPU statevector jobs versus qsim versus PennyLane default.qubit, because these produce different textual patterns and failure modes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the canonicalized backend bucket produced by the new ingestion schema, where several simulator implementations across projects are collapsed into one normalized 'simulator' field.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'simulator backend' sounds precise enough and both know the projects are simulator-heavy; because the canonicalized field has the same label as the raw concept, the false consensus survives normal conversation.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to fix the detector
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'stabilize the detector before the demo.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks stabilization means recovering the prior precision/false-positive behavior on the held-out benchmark slice used in internal evaluation, even if production alert counts stay somewhat elevated for a day.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks stabilization means bringing the live volume of 'likely flaky' flags back to a normal operational range for triage consumers, even if that is achieved by temporary filtering or grouping changes that alter benchmark comparability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely trying to reduce noise quickly, and 'stabilize' is a natural troubleshooting word; because demo-readiness and production calm usually correlate, neither notices they are using different acceptance tests.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention preserving the 'environment details' from bug reports while cleaning template noise.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the full textual environment section remains available to feature extraction, including phrases like 'shots=1024', seed notes, CUDA driver mentions, and simulator-specific options embedded in free text.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'environment details' means only structured metadata fields extracted from that section are retained, while the original prose and repeated template text can be dropped after normalization.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe they are preserving environment information, just at different levels of granularity; 'environment details' is broad enough to naturally cover either raw text or extracted fields, so the mismatch feels like an implementation detail rather than something worth clarifying in a troubleshooting call.

turns.inner_thought: The jump is too abrupt to be a real behavior change across all those repos overnight. If the ingestion rollout changed what counts as a rerun, my consistency features could be comparing executions that were never meant to be evidence of flakiness. For me, reruns only matter when it's the same workflow on the same commit with effectively the same dependency state. I really don't want to back out the new calibration before the demo unless I can show the detector is reacting to shifted inputs.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. We had a pretty sharp overnight spike in 'likely flaky' labels across Aer, Cirq, and PennyLane, well past the normal band. Before I touch the detector, I want to understand whether reruns are being interpreted differently after the latest rollout.

turns.inner_thought: This is probably the unification rollout making related executions line up more consistently, not a real defect. Our lineage now groups nearby executions under the same incident even if a patch version, seed default, or container changed slightly, which is fine for triage. And the backend field is finally canonicalized, so all the simulator-family reports land together. I need to defend the rollout without sounding territorial.
turns.utterance: Yeah, the unification changes went live yesterday. Reports tied to the same issue should now share a cleaner rerun lineage, and the backend metadata is more normalized than before. So some cases are probably lining up in the incident store that used to stay split by repo-specific ingestion paths.

turns.inner_thought: The biggest concentration is on what I think of as the specific execution targets in the raw reports, and those behaved very differently in training. Aer CPU wording is not qsim wording, and neither looks like default.qubit text. Also, rerun inconsistency only meant something when the exact same job flipped outcomes without any other changes. If those notions got broadened, the model would absolutely overfire.
turns.utterance: The biggest jump on my side is concentrated on the simulator backend. In prior training data, those reports only tended to look flaky when the same failing job alternated outcomes across reruns, so that's the part I'm trying to reconcile.

turns.inner_thought: Environment details are preserved in the right way: the extracted configuration is still there, and we dropped repetitive prose after normalization. Better to keep this high level so she hears that the important information is still present.
turns.utterance: The environment details are still preserved. What changed is mostly that the new parser extracts the core environment configuration and strips boilerplate template text, so the records are cleaner but the signal should still be there.

Good—this gives me a plausible explanation that isn't 'the upgrade was bad.'
turns.utterance: Yeah, that could still shift behavior. If the detector is seeing reports as cleaner but less specific, ordinary nondeterminism language might start reading like stronger flakiness evidence than it used to.

turns.inner_thought: Maybe, but the urgent thing is the alert curve. Triage consumers are getting flooded today. Stabilizing before the demo means bringing production volume back into a normal range quickly, ideally with an ingestion-side mitigation so nobody asks to revert the rollout.
turns.utterance: That's possible, but the live issue right now is the alert surge itself. We need to stabilize the detector before the demo, and I'd rather reduce the current production spike quickly while we sort out the underlying cause.
